Alaska – Halibut Fish & Chips

Welcome to The Last Frontier and another Great Plate! 

Britain’s iconic 1860s fish and chips sails north to Alaska where the fishing roots run deep, and legendary Pacific halibut caught from the cold North Pacific, known for its mild, sweet flavor and thick, meaty bite is used for this Alaskan staple.. While cod built the tradition, halibut takes it to a richer, heartier level, delivering a golden, premium spin on a timeless classic. 

Beer-battered, golden, flaky Alaskan halibut, straight from the cold northern waters is served with hand-cut fries tossed in our secret fry seasoning,  made-from-scratch tartar sauce, classic malt vinegar, and a bright lemon wedge for that perfect coastal finish.

This week’s dish is flaky, golden, and flirting with perfection. Order the halibut.

$17.95

12/24/2025 – 12/28//2025

 Texas – Chicken Fried Steak & White Peppery Gravy

Welcome to The Lone Star State and another Great Plate! 

Pull up a chair and loosen your belt. This one’s pure Texas folklore on a plate. Chicken Fried Steak is Texas comfort with immigrant roots. German and Austrian settlers brought schnitzel know-how in the 1800s, Texans swapped fancy veal for tough local beef, pounded it tender, breaded it, fried it like chicken, and called it a win.There’s no chicken involved. It’s “chicken-fried” because the method matches fried chicken. The real star is the peppery white cream gravy, poured on thick and proud. Over time, CFS went from hard-times cooking to Texas icon, name-checked in books, loved in diners, and even recognized by the Texas legislature. Chicken fried means white gravy, country fried means brown, and Texas knows exactly which side it’s on.

Chicken Fried Steak done the Texas way. Tender cube steak, double-breaded and fried till it’s crunchier than a gravel road in August, parked next to house-made mashed potatoes and drowned in peppery white gravy. No chicken, no apologies, just a fork-tender legend that eats like a love letter to your taste buds straight from Texas

 No chicken, all Texas. Come get yourself a proper Chicken Fried Steak. What cha waitin’ for?!

$17.95

 Arkansas – Biscuits & Chocolate Gravy

Welcome to The Natural State and another Great Plate

Born in the hill-hugging kitchens of the South, this dish is a proud child of the Ozarks, where the foodways zigzag as boldly as the mountain ridgelines. Folks say it really took off during the lean years of the Great Depression, when clever cooks rummaged through the pantry and spun everyday staples like cocoa, flour, milk, sugar, and a splash of saved-up fat into something warm and filling. For many Arkansans, it’s a legacy in a skillet, passed down from grandma’s flour-dusted notebook. And… when it eventually found its way to Graceland, it didn’t just get served. It sashayed right into Southern culinary folklore, claiming its place as a regional treasure.

Two jumbo buttermilk biscuits arrive looking like they’ve been caught in a joyful chocolate downpour, each one soaked in Pepaw Grimes’s silky, secret-family-treasure gravy. The buttermilk crumb stays tender and warm beneath that glossy cocoa cascade, turning every bite into a little breakfast celebration 

Come on in and taste an Arkansas legend: biscuits swimming in warm chocolate delight.

 $16.50

  Montana –  Nutburger

Welcome to The Big Sky Country and another Great Plate.

The Nutburger is pure Butte magic that was born in the 1930s at Montana’s very first drive-in, Matt’s Place. Legend says Matt himself tried a mayo-and-peanut burger in California and thought, “Well heck, we can do that better,” and he did.

Odd? Maybe. Beloved? Absolutely.
It became a Montana classic, even winning a James Beard America’s Classic Award. Matt’s Place closed for a spell, but in 2025 the landmark reopened, and the famous Nutburger strutted right back onto the grill where it belongs.

Our Montana Nutburger stacks two perfectly seasoned beef smash patties, all cozied up under a sweet-tangy Miracle Whip sauce loaded with toasted, crushed salted peanuts. It’s tucked into a warm toasted brioche bun, makin’ the whole thing taste like small-town charm and big-sky comfort in every bite.

This burger is a little quirky, a lot delicious, and pure Big Sky delight. In short, it works for the taste buds. Come in and see for yourself.

  $15.95

 Delaware – The Bobby Sandwich or Thanksgiving on a Roll

Welcome to The First State and another Great Plate.

Delaware’s famous Bobbie sandwich was basically born from one brilliant family tradition: raiding the Thanksgiving leftovers. Capriotti’s founders, siblings Lois and Alan Margolet, loved their Aunt Bobbie’s day-after-Thanksgiving turkey-stuffing-cranberry masterpieces so much, they put them on the menu in their first Wilmington shop. The result? “Thanksgiving on a roll,” a.k.a. the Bobbie, the sandwich that’s been praised by Esquire, the Food Network, and even crowned “The Greatest Sandwich in America.”  AND… it is served year-round. Not bad for leftovers!

Our Bobbie Sandwich isn’t just a sandwich… it’s a full-blown holiday miracle you can hold in one hand. Cold or hot, it starts with tender smoked turkey, a glorious mix of white and dark meat, piled high like we’re daring gravity to stop us. Then comes our family-recipe stuffing, and house-made cranberry chutney so good you’ll consider writing it a love letter. All of this delicious chaos is tucked inside a soft, local Bread Shop hoagie roll that’s been lovingly slathered with mayo and paired with a side of from-scratch turkey gravy built specifically for guilt-free dunking.

Hungry? The Bobbie is calling. Answer it. It's Thanksgiving flavor fireworks!

 $18.95

Wyoming – Bison Chili & a Cinnamon Roll

Welcome to The Equality State and another Great Plate.

Bison chili is Wyoming in a bowl hearty, local, and just ranch-y enough to make you say “yee-haw.” Chugwater’s famous chili seasoning has won so many cook-offs it practically has its own fan club. As for the legendary chili plus cinnamon roll combo? Nobody’s totally sure. Maybe it started in early logging camps where cooks served whatever kept laborers full. Others say the 1946 school lunch program, where lunch ladies discovered kids would happily eat chili if it came with a giant frosted bribe. Regardless, Wyomingites either dunk their cinnamon rolls straight into the chili like fearless pioneers… or keep them politely separated like they’re on a first date.

Our hearty bison chili starts with lean ground bison from Dr. King’s Carolina Bison in Asheville, NC, simmered with onions, peppers, black beans, and stewed tomatoes in a bold blend of our secret spices. We pile it high with cheddar cheese, fresh jalapeños, green onions, and a dollop of sour cream. And because life should always have a little sweetness, it comes with one of our made-from-scratch cinnamon rolls—soft, warm, and slathered with cream cheese icing—served on the side for dipping, mixing, or savoring all on its own.

Swing by! Treat yourself to big flavors, bold bison, and a cinnamon roll that’ll steal your heart.

 $17.95

Vermont – Chicken Pie

Welcome to The Green Mountain State and another Great Plate!

In Vermont, chicken pie has always been about simplicity and practicality. Back in the day, farmers didn’t waste a thing. When the old hens stopped laying eggs, they went straight into the pot. Those birds were tough, so they had to be slow-cooked until tender enough to fall apart. By the late 1800s, Vermonters decided to ditch the traditional pie crust and top their chicken pie with flaky biscuit dough instead. It was quicker, heartier, and, let’s face it, much less fussy. And unlike most potpies, you won’t find a single pea or carrot hiding in a Vermont chicken pie. It’s just chicken and gravy…rich, simple, and unapologetically old-fashioned. 

Tender, slow-poached chicken, swimming in rich, velvety gravy made from our own scratch-made chicken stock, then crowned with buttery homemade biscuits baked ‘til the tops are golden, flaky, and begging to be broken into.  

It’s cozy, comforting, and downright irresistible just like a warm Vermont hug straight out of the oven.

$15.95

Missouri – Toasted Ravioli or T-ravs

Welcome to The Show-Me State and another Great Plate!

Back in the 1940s, in St. Louis’s Italian-American neighborhood The Hill, someone made one of the most glorious culinary whoopsies in food history. Two restaurants still argue about who did it first. At Charlie Gitto’s (then Angelo’s) legend has it, a frazzled chef dropped ravioli into a pot of hot oil instead of boiling water one busy night in 1947. Instead of crying over spilt marinara, they served it up, and the crowd went wild! Mama’s on The Hill (then Oldani’s) story is even juicier. They claim a cook (possibly a little tipsy) made the same mistake… or maybe a German cook, Fritz, just misunderstood “drop some ravioli” and went straight for the fryer. Either way, the ravioli came out golden and crunchy, and everyone agreed: mistakes taste delicious.

Lemme tell ya somethin’, hon, this ain’t no store-bought ravioli situation. Our chefs went all out, makin’ that dough from scratch, just like Nonna on The Hill. Stuffed it full of ricotta, mozzarella, and parmesan because one cheese just ain’t enough, ya know? Then we bread it, toast it up nice and crispy, golden brown. Comes with our house-made marinara for dippin’, and if you’re feelin’ fancy, we got some pesto too.

It’s crunchy, cheesy, and pure St. Louis comfort. The kinda meal that makes ya say, “Oh yeah, that’s the good stuff, right there.”

$17.95

 South Dakota – Indian Taco

Welcome to The Mount Rushmore State and another Great Plate!

Now this is how South Dakota does taco night! Piled high on golden, puffy fry bread (not some crunchy store-bought shell) this is comfort food with a story. Back in the late 1800s, when American Indians were relocated to reservations, they were rationed simple ingredients like flour, salt, lard, and powdered milk. In South Dakota, they got yeast instead of baking soda, so naturally, they made fry bread rise to the occasion. Today, that same recipe holds strong, a little crispy, a little fluffy, and a whole lot of heart. 

We start with our house-made South Dakota fry bread, yep, the official state bread. Golden, fluffy, and just the right amount of crispy around the edges. We top it with seasoned ground beef (or, for the veggie folks, our seasoned black beans). Then we pile on diced tomatoes, onions, green chilis, shredded cheddar, a little iceberg for crunch, and a good ol’ dollop of sour cream to seal the deal.

From resilience to recipe, it’s a South Dakota story told on fry bread. Every bite is a nod to strength, resourcefulness, and good eatin’.

$17.95

Oh ya, up in North Dakota, they don’t just eat a hot beef sandwich, and we respect it, don’tcha know. Folks up there call it a “hot beef commercial,” though nobody’s quite sure why maybe ‘cause it’s so good it oughta be on TV, ya betcha.

Oh ya, this here’s a real North Dakota classic, dontcha know, Hot Beef Open-Face Sandwich! We start with toasted sourdough, ‘cause plain ol’ bread just can’t handle this kinda action. Then we pile on the tender slow-cooked pot roast. Next to that, you’ve got our fresh rosemary-garlic potatoes, yup, rosemary right from our own little herb garden out back. Then, the grand finale… our brown gravy, made from scratch, not that packet nonsense. You can have it smothered on top or in a little bowl on the side if you’re feelin’ fancy, but either way, once that gravy hits your plate, it’s game over. 

One bite and you’ll be sayin’, ‘Uff da, I’m not sharin’ this plate!

Indiana – Breaded Tenderloin Sandwich

Welcome to The Hoosier State and another Great Plate.

Well, bless your Hoosier heart, the breaded pork tenderloin sandwich is Indiana on a bun. Born at Nick’s Kitchen way back in 1908, Nick Freienstein took a fancy Austrian-German Wiener Schnitzel, swapped the veal for local pork (because, of course he did), and fried it up golden brown. He started selling those beauties from a little food cart, and next thing you know, every diner from Terre Haute to Fort Wayne was serving a Breaded Tenderloin Sandwich which is now known as the unofficial state sandwich. 

Get a taste of true Hoosier happiness. Juicy pork tenderloin, pounded thin, breaded with good old saltine crackers, and fried golden-crisp (just the way Grandma did it) served on a toasted brioche bun topped off with crunchy pickles, red onion, and a good squiggle of yellow mustard. 

It’s crispy, it’s juicy, and it’s the pride of Indiana unofficially, officially. You’re gonna want some of this!

Kansas – The Z-Man Sandwich

Welcome to The Sunflower State and another Great Plate!

The Z-Man sandwich was born in the late ’90s when Joe’s Kansas City Bar-B-Que pitmaster Jeff Stehney teamed up with local sports radio star Mike “The Z-Man” Zarrick. Zarrick wanted a sandwich worthy of his nickname, so Stehney stacked slow-smoked brisket, provolone, crispy onion rings, and barbecue sauce on a Kaiser roll…and barbecue history was made. A naming contest flopped, but everyone just kept asking for “the Z-Man,” and the name (and legend) stuck.

Now this here’s Kansas City done right tender Wagyu, brisket from Pittsboro’s own O’Quinn’s Butchery, (yes, we said Wagyu & O’Quinn’s because we do not fool around when it comes to quality) smoked low and slow in-house for a good twelve hours till it’s melt-in-your-mouth perfect. We slice it thin, pile it high on a fresh Kaiser roll, drizzle it with our made-from-scratch Kansas City BBQ sauce, lay on some smoky provolone, and crown it all with crispy onion rings. 

The Z-Man: where brisket dreams come true and diets go to die happy. If you love smoked brisket, this is your week Z-Man’s on deck and it’s pure BBQ glory.

 $19.95

 Mississippi – Traditional Tamale

Welcome to The Magnolia State and another Great Plate!

Greenville is the hot bed of tamale country, y’all! Nobody’s really sure if the recipe rolled in with Mexican field workers or bubbled up from cush, an old African American dish, but one thing’s for certain: the Delta grabbed hold of hot tamales and never let go. For generations, folks have been wrapping up spicy little bundles, perfect for tucking in your pocket and keeping warm during chilly cotton-picking days. After the harvest, street corners lit up with pushcarts and stands, vendors hollering and handing out tamales by the dozen. These days, it’s still the African American families of the Delta who keep the magic alive, serving up tamales with all the soul, spice, and joy the Mississippi Delta is famous for.   

A soft masa dough, stuffed full of slow-cooked verde chicken, all wrapped up snug in a corn husk and steamed ‘til it’s tender as can be. We top it off with our fresh-made pico and serve it alongside a side of our house verde sauce… zesty, and downright Delta delicious. 

Wrapped up with love, spice, and that Mississippi magic! You have GOT to try it!

$13.95

 Rhode Island – Clam Cakes

Welcome to The Ocean State and another Great Plate!

Rhode Island clam cakes have been around way before Aunt Carrie made ’em famous in 1920. Local folks were frying up quahogs back in the 1800s because when life gives you too many quahogs, you toss ’em in dough and fry ’em up. What started as a thrifty way to handle clam overload turned into the Ocean State’s ultimate comfort food. 

Crispy on the outside, fluffy on the inside stuffed with juicy clams, chives, a splash of beer, and a kiss of spice. They are fried golden, and served up with our own tartar sauce, malt vinegar, and a lemon wedge.  

Dunk ’em, squeeze ’em, love ’em! These little cakes are chowda’s best buddy and Rhode Island’s pride and joy.

Welcome to The Badger State and another Great Plate!!

This week we’re serving up a double dose of Dairyland glory… fried cheese curds and a Wisconsin Beer Burger! Back in the 1800s, cheesemakers snacked curds right outta the vat (perks of the job). Meanwhile in Seymour, 1885, “Hamburger Charlie” slid a beef patty between bread at the county fair so folks could eat and walk at the same time. Washington State – Smoked Salmon Toast

Welcome to The Evergreen State and another Great Plate!!

For thousands of years, Native tribes in the Pacific Northwest smoked salmon to keep it flavorful and lasting, each with their own special touch. Salmon became more than food; it shaped culture, tradition, and community. It’s so cherished that in 1987 Washington even tried to make a smoked salmon sandwich the official state snack. 

Smoked Salmon Toast on warm, crusty La Farm sourdough, piled with silky wild-caught cold-smoked salmon, a dreamy layer of cream cheese, and a sprinkle of briny capers. Finished with our pickled red onions and a fresh little dill sprig—it’s as tasty as it is pretty.

 The Pacific Northwest, served on sourdough. Stop by to catch Washington’s flavor in every bite.

 New Mexico – Stacked Enchiladas

Welcome to The Land of Enchantment and another Great Plate!!

Enchiladas trace back to the Aztecs, but in New Mexico they took on a style all their own. Instead of rolled, they’re stacked layer upon layer, smothered in bold red or green chile (often Hatch, of course). Rooted in Indigenous, Spanish, and Mexican traditions, New Mexican enchiladas are history served hot on a plate. 

Forget rolling, we are stacking ‘em sky-high, layer after layer. Start with browned beef (or refried beans, we’ve got love for the vegetarians), sizzle up some onions, add a pinch of chile powder, then toss in chopped Hatch chiles for that signature kick. Now the fun begins: stack a crunchy tortilla, pile on the goodness, meat or beans, melty cheese, house-made enchilada sauce. Then we do it again… and again… and again. Finally, crown it all with more cheese, a few of our last fresh tomatoes of the season, some crunchy shredded iceberg lettuce and 2 eggs cooked any way you like.

It’s messy, it’s cheesy, it’s chile heaven in a pan. Warning: our stacked enchiladas may cause fork fights at the table.

 $16.95

Nebraska – Runza Sandwich

Welcome to the Corn Husker State and another Great Plate!!

The Runza may have Russian-German roots, but it truly found its home on the Nebraska plains. Back in 1949, Sally Everett fired up a little cinder block stand in Lincoln, serving up these meat-and-cabbage stuffed rolls that warm you up more than a Huskers win. Her son, Don, took it big-time in the ‘60s, and today Sally’s grandson keeps the family tradition going.

Our Runza Sandwich is pure Nebraska comfort with soft, house-made pocket bread stuffed with savory ground beef, sweet yellow onion, and fresh green cabbage, all seasoned with our little secret spice blend. A warm, cozy hug for your belly. Served with ketchup and/or mustard on the side.

Runza. Nebraska born, Nebraska proud; a house-made bread pocket of LOVE! Come try one.

The Virginia ham biscuit is a true historical gem, predating the biscuit itself by centuries! Straight from the old country (the Basque region, that magical land tucked between Spain and France), but with a Nevada attitude—bold, flavorful, and not afraid to get a little smoky.

Michigan – Wet Burrito

Oklahoma – Okie Burger

Welcome to the Sooner State and another Great Plate!!

The Oklahoma onion burger got its start in El Reno back in 1926, when Ross Davis at the Hamburger Inn figured out how to stretch a buck during the Great Depression. Beef was high-dollar, onions were dirt cheap, so ol’ Ross slapped a thin patty on the griddle, piled it high with onions, and smashed it flat. Them onions caramelized right into the meat, and it was downright delicious. The original joint’s long gone, but the tradition’s still kickin’.

Small’s Okie Burger ain’t shy—it’s two juicy patties jam-packed with onions, smashed together caramelizing those onions right on into it. Topped with a gooey slice of American cheese and hugged by a warm, steamed potato bun. Comes with chips on the side, ‘cause we don’t need no frills when we’ve got flavor this big.

Perfect for the 4th of July? Shoot, this burger’s so American it probably sings the national anthem while you chow down, AND….it’s Oklahoma-famous—simple, scrappy, and full of flavor, just like the folks who love ’em.

Maryland - Crab Cakes

Welcome to the Old Line State and another Great Plate!! 

Sure, picking crabs around a newspaper-covered table is peak Maryland—but when you want less mess and more yum, crab cakes are the move. These beauties date back to Chesapeake Native American tribes, who started the whole hand-picking tradition we still use today. The settlers got hooked, and the rest is crabby history. In Maryland, a proper crab cake is mostly lump, barely filler, and always full of Old Bay pride.

Maryland-style crab cakes are the real deal—jumbo lump crab (none of that mystery mix), touched with a bit of Old Bay, lemon juice, mayo, fresh herbs, and a dab of stone ground mustard for good measure. We pan-fry them to golden perfection, then fancy things up with a side of remoulade—because even crab cakes like to get dressed up sometimes.

You’re gettin’ lump crab in every single bite of this crab cake—no fillers, no funny business. Still skeptical? Bless your heart. We dare you to take a bite and tell us otherwise. Go on… we’ll wait.

Maine – Lobster Roll

Welcome to The Pine Tree State and another Great Plate! 

Once upon a tide, in the crusty old 1920s, a little seafood joint in Milford, Connecticut, called Perry’s claimed to have invented the lobster roll. Bold move, Perry. Bold move. But while Connecticut may have rolled first, it was Maine that clawed its way to greatness when Maine’s lobstermen took one look at that humble hot dog bun, gave it a buttery tan on the grill, and thought, "You know what this needs? An avalanche of lobster." And thus, the true lobster roll as we know it today was born. 

This isn’t just a lobster roll—it’s a love letter from the coast of Maine.  A little history about the Philly Cheesesteak. Pat and his brother Harry were just a couple of guys running a humble hot dog stand in South Philly, near the Italian Market. But Pat? He was over the whole "hot dog for lunch" routine. So, one day, he decided to throw some beef and onions on the grill instead. Enter Dave Kohn, a cab driver cruising by, who took one bite and said, “This is it! You’ve gotta sell these!” And just like that, the sandwich started catching on. Fast forward to the 1940s, and a manager at the Olivieri’s Ridge Ave. spot thought, “You know what this needs? Provolone!” And boom, the cheesesteak was born. Now, Pat’s King of Steaks—the OG—has been family-run ever since. In Philly, cheesesteak is a serious local tradition—complete with rivalry between Pat’s and Geno’s Steaks, located just across the street from each other. 

 Get ready to meet the Philly Cheesesteak of your dreams: piled high on a soft hoagie roll, bursting with tender, thinly sliced sirloin, caramelized onions, zesty red and green bell peppers, gooey provolone cheese, and a drizzle of herb aioli that’ll have your taste buds doing a happy dance. North Carolina - BBQ Sandwich…Lexington Style!

Welcome home to First in Flight State; another GreatState & another Great Plate! In North Carolina, barbecue is a noun not a verb. It’s something you add red or white slaw to and chow down. It plays an important part in the history, heritage, family dinner tables and kitchens across the state.

We are all familiar with the GREAT BBQ DEBATE over western(i.e, Lexington BBQ) verses Eastern BBQ. What’s the difference and why is western BBQ called Lexington style? The difference in taste is all in the sauce. Lexington has a tomato or ketchup vinegar base which gives a redder, sweet, tangy flavor while eastern has a vinegar and pepper base which tastes salty, fiery, and vinegary on the palate. The name Lexington style comes from Sid Weaver and Jeff Swicegood, who are revered as the first owners of a stand-alone barbecue establishment located there in the seat of Davison County.

Our BBQ Sandwich has 8 hour slow cooked pork shoulder rubbed in an original house-made spice blend, tossed in our Lexington style BBQ sauce and topped with red slaw, not because we added a little sauce to it, but because it is a Sriracha Coleslaw that adds a slight spiciness to our made-from-scratch recipe.

California-Avocado Toast

Welcome to the Golden State and another Great Plate! The beloved Avocado Toast is not a new trend. Oh Nooo, in the San Francisco Bay Area, people have been eating avocado toast since at least 1885. In 1915, the California Avocado Association described serving small squares of avocado toast as an appetizer. It’s been called alligator pear and midshipmans’ butter, but in 1993 the Instagrammable avocado toast served at fashionable all-day cafés, Bills in Sydney, Australia is where it got its start. Bill Granger is credited with the first to ever put avocado toast on a menu, but seventeen years after Granger opened Bills, a young, relatively unknown American chef named Jessica Koslow showed up in Melbourne to soak in Australia’s modern café culture. She returned to her birthplace, L.A, and.  opened Sqirl, a daytime restaurant in the Australian model. Koslow created her own version of avocado toast topped with a worldly assortment betraying her professional cooking background: garlic cream, pickled-carrot curls, sumac, and sesame seeds.  This would be a pivotal moment. Putting serious cooking techniques behind trendy wellness food, Sqirl set the stage for a new kind of American restaurant. Let the avocado toast craze begin!!

Small’s version of Avocado Toast starts with crusty pieces of Ciabatta from La Farm slathered with cream cheese and  mashed avocado blended with red pepper flakes, everything bagel seasoning and lime juice topped off with some slices of avocado and an egg made any way you would like.
